tldr: Spatial-UMI-Dream integrates stereo-derived metric depth into handheld gripper (UMI) demonstrations, creating a 5B spatial World Action Model that jointly predicts future RGB-D video and robot actions. It achieves significantly higher success rates and superior cross-robot embodiment transfer than strong existing VLAs and WAMs across simulation and real-world bimanual tasks.
hero_caption: Overall architecture and two-stage training pipeline of Spatial-UMI-Dream. RGB and metric depth from both wrist cameras are arranged onto a single canvas. Built on the Wan2.2 video foundation model, it is trained progressively through world-only adaptation followed by joint world-action learning.
overview:
The Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) is a breakthrough system that enables scalable demonstration collection via human-operated handheld grippers without requiring a physical robot present. However, its wrist-mounted wide-angle fisheye cameras move aggressively alongside the hands. As a result, visual changes entangle camera ego-motion, object motion, and the underlying 3D depth structure of the scene. Conventional World Action Models (WAMs)—which predict future RGB frames alongside actions—must infer 3D absolute distances and scene scale (metric geometry) implicitly from RGB appearance alone. Consequently, they tend to fail during precision grasping and handovers that demand millimeter-level alignment.

To address this challenge, the authors developed Spatial-UMI-Dream, a spatial World Action Model that reconstructs real-scale metric depth from gripper-mounted stereo cameras, tiles it alongside RGB frames onto a single canvas, and feeds/predicts it with a video foundation model (Wan2.2-TI2V-5B). Leveraging a 605-hour RGB-D UMI dataset, the model is trained with a two-stage recipe: "world-only adaptation" to accustom the model to dynamic fisheye viewpoints and RGB-D canvas predictions, followed by "joint world-action learning" to jointly predict actions.

Furthermore, to rigorously test whether demonstrations collected independently of a robot can generalize across different robot embodiments, the authors introduced RoboTwin-UMI, a simulation benchmark spanning 20 manipulation tasks. On RoboTwin-UMI, Spatial-UMI-Dream achieved a 79.10% in-domain success rate and 72.15% under combined embodiment and lighting shifts, outperforming the strongest baseline by 10.30 percentage points. Across six real-world bimanual tasks, it reached an average success rate of 85.0%, demonstrating the overwhelming robustness and efficacy of incorporating spatial geometry into world action models.
contributions: Proposed Spatial-UMI-Dream, a 5B-parameter spatial World Action Model that integrates fisheye RGB and aligned metric depth from dual grippers onto a single video canvas to jointly predict future RGB-D and actions.
Established an efficient two-stage pretraining recipe using 605 hours of RGB-D UMI data, progressively adapting a video foundation model from world adaptation to joint world-action learning.
Introduced kinodynamic trajectory filtering to eliminate unfeasible demonstrations and command latency compensation to resolve physical gripper response delays.
Constructed RoboTwin-UMI, a 20-task simulation benchmark for evaluating zero-shot policy generalization under embodiment and environmental lighting shifts, both separately and jointly.

sections.heading: Why Predict Real-Scale Geometry Alongside RGB Video?
sections.summary: Handheld UMI demonstration collection is scalable, but aggressive wrist camera motion makes estimating accurate 3D scale from RGB alone very difficult. This paper introduces Spatial-UMI-Dream, a 5B model that integrates metric depth directly into a world model, alongside RoboTwin-UMI, a new benchmark to evaluate embodiment transfer and environmental generalization.
sections.details:
In learning autonomous robot manipulation, two paradigms have gained significant traction: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs), which directly map vision and language to actions, and World Action Models (WAMs), which jointly predict future visual changes and actions. WAMs are especially compelling because they leverage physical and motion priors from video diffusion models to predict how the environment responds to robot actions.

However, applying existing WAMs to data collected with handheld grippers via the Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) presents two major hurdles:

- **RGB images alone lack 3D spatial scale**: UMI lacks static, third-person overhead cameras; it relies solely on wrist-mounted fisheye cameras. Because the cameras move rapidly with the grippers, visual changes entangle camera ego-motion and object motion. In bimanual manipulation, where both arms move independently while coordinating in a shared 3D workspace, estimating millimeter-level distances from RGB appearance alone is notoriously difficult.
- **A lack of rigorous evaluation for cross-robot embodiment transfer**: UMI's primary advantage is that humans can collect data without needing a specific robot. To assess its true value, one must evaluate whether learned policies can directly transfer to different robot embodiments and novel lighting conditions.

To solve these problems, the authors propose Spatial-UMI-Dream, which incorporates metric depth (absolute real-world distance) recovered from stereo cameras alongside RGB as inputs and prediction targets for a world model. Additionally, they introduce RoboTwin-UMI, a benchmark designed to exhaustively evaluate zero-shot transfer across two distinct robot embodiments and dynamic lighting variations.

sections.heading: The Evolution of Robot Foundation Models, 3D Geometry, and UMI
sections.summary: Prior robot foundation models either focused purely on action prediction or limited future predictions to RGB video. This work takes a unified approach, treating metric depth directly as a prediction target for the world model without requiring an explicit external 3D encoder.
sections.details:
### Trends in Robot Foundation Models and World Action Models
Prominent robot foundation models to date (such as $\pi_0$ and other VLAs) have employed an action-centric design, predicting action tokens directly from vision and language. However, this structure does not explicitly capture the causal relationship of how actions alter the surrounding scene. Recently, methods predicting future visual frames for planning and World Action Models (WAMs) that jointly generate future vision and actions have emerged. Yet conventional WAMs remain restricted to RGB images, leaving absolute spatial dimensions and geometric structures implicit within internal model representations.

### Incorporating Geometric Structure into Robot Learning
Geometric information, such as point clouds or depth maps, is crucial for grasping and millimeter-level alignment. Existing research often relies on explicit 3D encoders to extract point cloud features or distills representations from pretrained 3D models into RGB policies. In contrast, Spatial-UMI-Dream uses neither dedicated 3D encoders nor distillation teacher models; instead, it incorporates aligned metric depth directly into the video canvas as an explicit state of the world to be predicted.

### UMI Data and Evaluation Benchmarks
While UMI unlocked robot-agnostic data collection, prior evaluations were often limited to success rates within a single environment. RoboTwin-UMI provides a standardized, reproducible simulation platform to evaluate UMI's core promises—robustness to environmental variations and cross-robot embodiment transfer—under identical task and camera specifications.

sections.heading: Unified Metric RGB-D Canvas and Two-Stage Training Pipeline
sections.summary: Stereo-reconstructed metric depth is colormapped and combined with RGB into a 2x2 canvas fed into the Wan2.2 video foundation model. Training proceeds in two stages—world adaptation followed by joint world-action learning—accompanied by control compensation to counteract physical execution delays.
sections.details:
### III-A Metric RGB-D Representation Construction
Each gripper is equipped with three cameras, where the center and right cameras form a stereo pair. Images are first undistorted and rectified based on epipolar geometry. Fast FoundationStereo then estimates disparity, which is converted to metric $Z$-depth. By unprojecting and reprojecting back into the center camera's fisheye frame, the system obtains a metric depth map $D_t^e$ that is pixel-aligned with the RGB image.

This depth is normalized across the dataset within a fixed range ($d_{\min}=0.01$ m, $d_{\max}=1.5$ m) and converted to a 3-channel image using the Turbo colormap. The left and right RGB images and colormapped depth images are arranged into a $2\times 2$ grid to form a single $320\times 320$ "unified canvas." This enables direct reuse of the pretrained Wan2.2 video VAE, processing geometric information without any specialized depth encoder.

### III-B Joint World-Action Modeling
The latent features of the unified canvas and the action tokens are fed into shared Transformer blocks. Conditioned on past visual sequences, the model employs bidirectional attention within the current world-action block to simultaneously denoise and predict future RGB-D canvases and action chunks via a flow-matching objective.

### III-C Two-Stage World-Action Pretraining
Using a 605-hour RGB-D UMI corpus, the model is trained in two steps:
- **Stage 1 (World-only adaptation)**: The action branch is detached, and the model is trained solely to predict future RGB-D canvases from past vision and language. This adapts the video foundation model to dynamic fisheye viewpoints and RGB-D canvas dynamics.
- **Stage 2 (Joint world-action training)**: The action encoder-decoder and robot state inputs are enabled. The world prediction loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{world}}$ and action prediction loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{action}}$ are jointly optimized with a weight $\lambda_a=1$.

### III-D Trajectory Filtering and Command Latency Compensation
Handheld demonstrations can contain kinematically infeasible trajectories that exceed physical robot joint limits or velocity bounds. Using inverse kinematics (IK) in ManiSkill, infeasible trajectories and the top 1% extreme episodes in velocity, acceleration, and jerk are filtered out. To counter real-world physical gripper delays, feedforward compensation derived from an inverted first-order lag model is applied, ensuring grips execute at the intended moments.

### III-E RoboTwin-UMI Benchmark
A 20-task benchmark was constructed in RoboTwin, faithfully replicating the UMI fisheye cameras and parallel grippers. It supports two dual-arm embodiments—Aloha (AgileX) and ARX-X5—under standard and randomized lighting conditions, allowing rigorous zero-shot transfer evaluation across four total configurations without policy fine-tuning.

sections.heading: Empirical Superiority in Precision and Cross-Embodiment Transfer
sections.summary: Evaluated across 20 RoboTwin-UMI simulation tasks and 6 real-world tasks, Spatial-UMI-Dream achieved the highest success rates in-domain and under unseen embodiment and lighting changes, substantially outperforming baselines in millimeter-precision tasks like bimanual handovers.
sections.details:
### IV-A Experimental Setup and Baselines
Real-world evaluations were conducted on a Dexmate Vega1 mobile dual-arm robot across six diverse tasks (20 trials each): plush toy placing, bimanual block handover, barcode scanning, packing, watering, and table wiping. Baselines included state-of-the-art VLAs ($\\pi_{0.5}$, RDT2-FM) and WAM baselines (Fast-WAM, LingBot-VA).

### IV-B In-Domain Performance
Across the six real-world tasks, Spatial-UMI-Dream achieved an average success rate of **85.0%**, outperforming the strongest baseline, $\\pi_{0.5}$ (60.8%), by 24.2 percentage points. On the "Bimanual Handover" task—which requires precise 3D localization as moving grippers exchange a wooden block—$\pi_{0.5}$ reached only 45.0%, whereas Spatial-UMI-Dream attained **80.0%**. Explicit metric depth provided the critical spatial cues needed for alignment.
In simulation (RoboTwin-UMI), Spatial-UMI-Dream achieved an in-domain success rate of **79.10%**, clearly exceeding $\\pi_{0.5}$ (74.45%) and the strongest WAM, Fast-WAM (61.20%).

### IV-C Embodiment Transfer and Environmental Generalization
When transferring policies trained on Aloha directly to the unseen ARX-X5 embodiment, $\\pi_{0.5}$ suffered a severe performance drop, whereas Spatial-UMI-Dream widened its lead to 14.00 percentage points. Under the most challenging condition combining embodiment transfer with randomized lighting, Spatial-UMI-Dream maintained a **72.15%** success rate, outperforming the closest baseline by 10.30 percentage points.
Qualitative error analysis showed that RGB-only Fast-WAM often stopped short of an alarm clock button or missed a coaster under lighting shifts, while Spatial-UMI-Dream maintained accurate approaches and contact grounded by depth.

### IV-D Ablation Studies: Value of Geometry and Two-Stage Learning
- **Impact of Depth**: Comparing against an RGB-only model (where RGB frames were duplicated to match token count), adding metric depth improved in-domain simulation success by 5.75 percentage points and combined shift success by 8.25 percentage points. In real-world trials, average success rose from 80.8% to 85.0%.
- **Impact of Two-Stage Training**: Directly fine-tuning the video foundation model on downstream tasks yielded only a 39.50% success rate. Adding world adaptation boosted it to 61.25%, and joint world-action pretraining further propelled it to **79.10%**.

sections.heading: How Spatial Geometry Shapes the Next Generation of Manipulation
sections.summary: By fusing the flexibility of handheld data collection with world models that predict metric depth, this work demonstrates that explicitly grounding pretraining in spatial geometry is vital for precision control and cross-robot transfer.
sections.details:
This paper presented Spatial-UMI-Dream, a 5B spatial World Action Model pretrained on 605 hours of RGB-D UMI data, alongside RoboTwin-UMI, a benchmark for evaluating cross-robot embodiment transfer and environmental generalization.

Even with aggressive camera ego-motion from wrist-mounted fisheye lenses, incorporating aligned metric depth into world model predictions dramatically boosts success rates in bimanual coordination and precision contact tasks. Furthermore, it maximizes the benefits of robot-agnostic data collection, minimizing performance drops when deploying policies onto unseen robot embodiments. Grounding world model pretraining in geometric representations offers a powerful design guideline for future generalist robot foundation models.

sections.heading: Appendix: Implementation Details and Simulation Benchmark Design
sections.summary: Covers Wan2.2 training and freezing configurations, pretraining hyperparameters, fisheye rendering via 4-view panoramic composition, and bimanual motion planning via PyRoKi in RoboTwin-UMI.
sections.details:
### Pretraining Hyperparameters and Optimization Setup
The base model is the pretrained Wan2.2-TI2V-5B. During training, all parameters of the video diffusion Transformer are updated, while the text encoder, image encoder, and video VAE remain frozen. The model is optimized using AdamW (learning rate $10^{-5}$, weight decay $10^{-5}$) with bfloat16 and DeepSpeed ZeRO-2 across 24 NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs for 30,000 steps per stage. Downstream fine-tuning uses 8 GPUs.

### RoboTwin-UMI Fisheye Synthesis and Bimanual Planning
To faithfully replicate real-world UMI fisheye cameras in simulation, scenes are rendered from four pinhole cameras sharing a common optical center (one forward at $92^\circ$, three peripheral at $106^\circ$). Images are then resampled into a $320\times 240$ fisheye projection using the Kannala–Brandt (KB4) distortion model.
For bimanual trajectory generation, a 12-DoF whole-body simultaneous optimization planner using PyRoKi and jaxls replaces traditional planners like MPLib. This automatically produces smooth, kinematically feasible demonstration trajectories that avoid self-collisions and environmental collisions while respecting velocity, acceleration, and jerk limits.

takeaways: Colormapping metric depth and tiling it alongside RGB on a single canvas allows standard video foundation models (WAMs) to model 3D geometry effectively without dedicated 3D encoders.
In wrist-camera setups with aggressive ego-motion, providing explicit absolute distances (geometry) is decisive for millimeter-level contact and grasping precision compared to RGB alone.
A two-stage pretraining recipe—progressing from world-only adaptation to joint world-action learning—substantially improves downstream task performance and cross-embodiment robustness.
When evaluating robot-agnostic demonstrations like UMI data, testing zero-shot generalization across unseen robot embodiments is just as essential as measuring in-domain success rates.
limitations: Because depth is reconstructed via stereo matching, depth estimates can degrade or exhibit noise on textureless flat surfaces, transparent objects, or highly reflective items.
Closed-loop inference with a 5B-parameter flow-matching diffusion model imposes noticeable computational demands and latency for high-frequency onboard control.
Embodiment transfer in the benchmark assumes identical gripper geometry and wrist camera configurations; transfer across radically different gripper designs or camera placements remains unverified.
